task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-07-13, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Lineup coverage (>=1 organizer, shaper, terminal) varies within team, is separable from talent/counts, and talent control behaves.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 420,993 possessions; 90 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: how to measure lineup coverage from possession-level play-type initiations and role categorizations
how to separate the effect of role coverage from overall player talent
how to control for talent while studying within-team lineup variation
whether within-team variation in role coverage is sufficient for identification

historical_evidence.finding: After talent control adapt p=0.275; n~55 series cannot separate coaching adaptation from roster quality.
Series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50, underpowered); still confounded by team quality.
Superstar suppression by lineup and forced play type; risk of PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE.
Lineup adds 0.0% to explanation of H1→H2 PPP collapse beyond RTM; residual 65.4% noise.
n>=15 gate suppresses real player-routing signal; low-n leaders have small-sample inflation.

failed_approaches.what_failed: attempt to separate adaptation quality from roster talent
failed_approaches.why: confounding by talent; sample too small (55 series)

failed_approaches.what_failed: AVOID share predicting winning after controlling for team quality
failed_approaches.why: confounding by team quality; underpowered (n=50 series)

evidence_establishes: Prior attempts to isolate non-talent team-level metrics (adaptation, AVOID share) from underlying talent have failed due to strong confounding and small effective sample sizes.
Lineup composition variables added negligible explanatory power for in-game PPP collapse when regression-to-the-mean was accounted for.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether lineup coverage by organizer, shaper, and terminal roles affects offensive or overall performance.
Whether such coverage is separable from average player talent in a within-team design.
The magnitude of within-team variation in role coverage across stints.
own_inferences: The research question is novel and has not been directly tested in the retrieved families.
The available data (play-by-play, play-type possessions, substitution intervals, role definitions) can in principle construct stint-level coverage indicators and talent controls.
A within-team identification strategy (team fixed effects, prior-season talent proxies, role definitions from prior data) is necessary to mitigate the confounding that plagued earlier work.
However, the risk remains that residual talent confounding or limited within-team coverage variation could make a conclusive test unattainable.
uncertainties: Stability and reliability of organizer[path] classifications for low-minute or role-transitioning players.
Availability and validity of out-of-sample talent metrics (e.g., prior-season RAPM) for all players in the analysis periods.
Degree of within-team variation in lineup coverage – if most teams rarely field a lineup missing a role, the test will be underpowered.
Potential collinearity between role coverage and other lineup characteristics (play-type mix, defensive matchups).

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence of failed attempts to separate adaptation/AVOID from talent ([prior work], [prior work]) warns that lineup-level metrics are easily confounded by team quality, so the original naive approach must be strengthened with within-team fixed effects and rigorous talent controls. Without this evidence, a design lacking such controls might have been considered sufficient.

blocking_constraints.text: Lineup coverage is likely correlated with average talent, as better teams may more often satisfy role coverage.
Within-team variation in coverage may be limited; many teams could have small cell sizes for non-covered lineups.
Role classification (organizer, shaper, terminal) uses structural influence metrics that vary across seasons and may be noisy for bench players.

prior_work.summary: No prior study examined the effect of lineup role coverage on performance. The closest work ([prior work], [prior work]) struggled to separate non-talent metrics from team quality, indicating the need for careful within-team identification.

risks.text: Talent confound: lineups with full role coverage may have higher average player talent, biasing naive comparisons.
Limited within-team variation may yield underpowered comparisons; many stints may be needed to achieve adequate power.
Role classification errors, especially for low-minute or role-changing players, could dilute or bias estimates.
Some teams may rarely or always exhibit full coverage, reducing usable within-team variation.
If roles are derived from the same season's data, there is lookahead bias; only prior-season or rolling historical data should be used.
If testing multiple seasons or secondary outcomes (net rating, playoff performance), corrections are needed.

design.estimand: The marginal effect on offensive points per possession (PPP) of a lineup having at least one organizer, one shaper, and one terminal simultaneously on the floor, relative to lineups missing at least one of these roles, controlling for average player talent and team-season fixed effects.
design.unit: A stint (interval of continuous play with the same ten players on the court), excluding garbage time.
design.sample: All regular-season stints from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 NBA seasons with valid role classifications and talent scores. Garbage time defined as 4th-quarter possessions when the absolute score margin exceeds 20 points.
design.power: Approximately 400,000 possessions aggregated into ~15,000 stints; within-team intraclass correlation expected ~0.05; minimum detectable effect of 0.02 PPP at 80% power for a two-sided test with team-clustered standard errors.
design.controls: Team-season fixed effects; average prior-season RAPM (or equivalent) of the five offensive players; number of starters in the lineup; rest days; home/away indicator; point differential at stint start (to account for game situation).
design.falsification: Permutation test: randomly reassign role labels within team to verify that the estimated effect disappears. Placebo test: replace actual talent control with shuffled talent scores and check that the coefficient changes accordingly. Test that the coverage variable is not correlated with opponent's average talent.
design.multiplicity: Primary outcome: offensive PPP, tested per season. Adjust p-values across seasons using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Secondary outcome: net rating (exploratory, reported without formal correction).
design.decision_rule: Two-sided p < 0.05 (adjusted) on the coverage coefficient in a linear mixed model with team-season fixed effects and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors clustered at the team level. Pre-register the model specification before data access.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular season data as of 2026-07-13.
